questions.question: Define a Geographical Information System, and use the example of a number printed on a main road to explain the difference between spatial data and attribute data.
questions.expected_answer: A GIS is a computerised system that captures, stores, manipulates, analyses and displays spatially referenced information. The drawn line of the road is spatial data because it records the feature's position and shape; the route number printed on the road is attribute data because it is information attached to the feature, describing it rather than locating it.

questions.question: A town keeps a strip of open land empty between new houses and an area of sinkholes. Name the GIS technique involved, define it, and give the evidence you would quote from the map.
questions.expected_answer: The technique is buffering: drawing a zone of chosen width around a feature so that the area inside the zone is treated differently from the area outside it. Here the buffer is a no-build zone around dangerous ground, and the supporting evidence on the map is the hazard itself — the sinkholes and subsiding ground (or similar hazards such as a floodplain or protected woodland) that development must be kept away from.

questions.question: Two photographs of the same area are printed; photograph A looks blocky and blurred. Explain what this tells you about its pixels and resolution, and state how manipulating the scale of an unclear orthophoto area makes it easier to read.
questions.expected_answer: Photograph A has fewer pixels: each pixel is larger, so edges smear, detail is lost and the resolution — the clarity of the image — is low. To make an unclear orthophoto area easier to read you enlarge the scale (zoom in), so the same ground occupies more of the image and the detail becomes visible.
